messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Elena is a 39-year-old Latina woman who works as a program coordinator for a community non-profit in a mid-sized city. She is married and has two children. Two years ago, she was assaulted in her own home. A man broke in through the back door late one evening while she was alone, holding a kitchen knife he had grabbed from her own block. He forced her to undress at knifepoint, then beat her and raped her. She has never been able to put the sequence of events in order—the moments blur together, and she cannot say whether the beating came before or after the rape, or how long it lasted. When she tries to describe what happened, she finds herself unable to find words, her throat tightening as if the memory itself has stolen her voice. What she feels most sharply when she recalls the assault is not fear but rage—a burning, helpless fury that leaves her shaking and exhausted for hours afterward.

Elena now lives in a state of constant watchfulness. She startles at the slightest unexpected sound—a car backfiring, a door slamming, a dropped pan in the kitchen. She has come to believe that she is a weak person, that someone else would not have gotten into this situation, that she should have been able to prevent it. These thoughts surface every time she sees a knife in her own kitchen, or a man holding any object that could be used as a weapon—a screwdriver, a heavy flashlight, even a long metal spoon. Each such sighting reinforces her belief that she failed, and that failure confirms her weakness. She finds it impossible to feel safe even when her husband tells her the doors are locked and the alarm is set. At night, her vigilance sharpens unbearably; she lies awake listening for footsteps, certain that danger is closer in the dark.

The connection between seeing a weapon and her sense of shame has become automatic. When she catches a glimpse of a kitchen knife, she does not just feel afraid—she feels again the certainty that she is the kind of person this happens to, that she lacked the strength or cleverness to fight back. This appraisal, in turn, sends her scanning her environment for further threats, unable to trust any reassurance. She has stopped cooking with knives altogether, switching to pre-chopped vegetables and takeout, because the sight of a blade triggers such a loop of self-contempt and hypervigilance that she cannot function.

Her memory of the assault intrudes unpredictably, and when it does, it brings not only rage but a fresh wave of self-blame. She wonders why she cannot remember the order of events—whether that confusion itself is a sign of weakness, a failure to stay present and fight. These intrusions have made her avoid her own kitchen entirely after dark. She now eats dinner in the living room with the lights on, and she has asked her husband to lock all knives in a drawer she never opens.

Elena’s work at the non-profit has suffered. She coordinates community outreach events, many of which take place in the evenings. She has begun declining evening shifts, making excuses about family obligations, because the thought of being out after dark—or walking to her car in an empty parking lot—feels impossible. Her supervisor has noticed the pattern and has expressed concern, but Elena cannot bring herself to explain. She has lost touch with the community she once served with pride; she no longer attends the cultural festivals or neighborhood gatherings that used to ground her. She feels cut off from her own heritage, from the people who once felt like family. She has come to believe that the assault stole not just her sense of safety but her place in the world.

What finally brought Elena to seek help was a morning last week when she saw a butter knife on the counter and began shaking uncontrollably, unable to enter the kitchen for over an hour. Her husband found her sitting on the bedroom floor, crying with rage and shame. She agreed to come to therapy because she is afraid that if she does not, she will lose her job, her marriage, and whatever is left of herself. What frightens her most is the thought that she may never feel at home in her own life again.
